subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

choices: Only the physical place where a species lives and feeds
The role of a species, including its habitat, interactions and resource use
The number of individuals of a species in an area
The highest trophic level a species reaches
items.note: Niche = how a species fits into its ecosystem: habitat, food, timing, interactions.

choices: Is poisoned by oxygen and can only respire anaerobically
Can respire with or without oxygen, depending on conditions
Requires oxygen for respiration
Uses light energy to make ATP
items.note: Obligate anaerobes die in oxygen; facultative anaerobes can switch; obligate aerobes need O₂.

choices: Ingesting living organisms and digesting them inside a gut
Making all their own carbon compounds by photosynthesis
Living inside a host and taking its food
Secreting enzymes onto dead matter and absorbing the products
items.note: External digestion of dead organic matter (e.g. many fungi and bacteria) recycles nutrients.

items.stem: Euglena can photosynthesise in light and ingest food in darkness. It is therefore:
choices: An obligate autotroph
A saprotroph
A mixotroph
A chemoautotroph
items.note: Mixotrophs combine autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition.

choices: Absorption of nutrients through the body surface only, without a gut
Synthesis of food using energy from light
Ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion
Breakdown of dead matter outside the body
items.note: Holozoic = ingesting food and digesting it internally, as in most animals.

items.stem: Herbivore teeth are often adapted with:
choices: Broad, flat molars for grinding plant material
Long, pointed canines for gripping and killing prey
Sharp carnassials for slicing meat
No molars at all
items.note: Plant material needs grinding to break cell walls. Canines and carnassials are carnivore features.

items.stem: Many plants produce toxic secondary compounds in their leaves. This is an adaptation to:
choices: Attract pollinators
Reduce herbivory
Increase photosynthesis
Store excess water
items.note: Chemical defences (e.g. alkaloids, tannins) deter or poison herbivores.

items.stem: The fundamental niche of a species is:
choices: The narrower niche it actually occupies when competitors are present
The habitat where its population is largest
The role it has in only one food chain
The full range of conditions and resources it could use without competitors
items.note: Competition, predation and other interactions usually restrict a species to a smaller realised niche.

items.stem: The competitive exclusion principle states that:
choices: Two species always share resources equally
The larger species always outcompetes the smaller
Competition between two species always leads to extinction of both of them
Two species cannot occupy the same niche indefinitely in the same place
items.note: One species will outcompete the other, unless their niches differ (resource partitioning).

choices: A group of eukaryotes that live only in extremely hot or salty habitats
A type of virus that infects bacteria
A domain of prokaryotes with diverse ways of obtaining energy
A kingdom of fungi that live in soils
items.note: Archaea include methanogens, halophiles and others using chemical or light energy; not all live in extremes.

items.stem: Two barnacle species live on rocky shores. Species A is found only in the upper zone, but if species B is removed from the lower zone, A also grows there. This shows that:
choices: Competition with B makes A's realised niche smaller than its fundamental niche
A cannot tolerate conditions in the lower zone
B's fundamental niche is limited to the upper zone of the rocky shore
Both species have identical realised niches on the rocky shore
items.note: A could live lower down (fundamental niche) but is excluded there by B — competition narrows A's realised niche.

items.stem: Compare the adaptations of a named predator and its prey.
markscheme: Predator adaptation named, e.g. forward-facing eyes for judging distance (1)
Prey adaptation named, e.g. eyes on side of head for wide field of view (1)
Further paired adaptation, e.g. speed/camouflage/warning colours (1)
Each linked to catching or avoiding capture (1)
items.tactic: Pair predator and prey features that are related.

items.stem: Outline the differences between autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition.
markscheme: Autotrophs make their own carbon compounds from inorganic sources (1)
Using energy from light (photo-) or chemical reactions (chemo-) (1)
Heterotrophs obtain carbon compounds from other organisms (1)
items.tactic: Use precise terms: inorganic carbon source vs organic food.

items.stem: Distinguish between fundamental and realised niches and explain how competition affects them.
markscheme: Fundamental niche: full potential range of conditions/resources a species could use (1)
Realised niche: the part actually occupied (1)
Competition from other species restricts the realised niche (1)
Competitive exclusion / resource partitioning allows coexistence (1)
items.tactic: Definitions first, then mechanism with an example if you have one.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Two invented flour beetle species were grown alone and together in containers at 30 °C for 120 days. Final population: species P alone 420; species Q alone 380; together P 410, Q 0.
(a) Describe the effect of growing the species together. (b) Explain the result using a named ecological principle. (c) Predict what might happen at a different temperature, and explain.
markscheme: (a) P barely changed (420 to 410) while Q was eliminated (380 to 0) (1)
(b) Competitive exclusion: both use the same resources/same niche; P outcompeted Q (1)
(c) Q might win/coexist at another temperature (1)
Because competitive ability depends on tolerance/optimum conditions for each species (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
